parts.title: From ticks to a weight
parts.brief: The EQ-5D describes a health state; a value set from the public turns it into a weight q.
parts.figure: Main figure: the EQ-5D-5L form as a grid — five rows named Mobility, Self-care, Usual activities, Pain/discomfort, Anxiety/depression, and five level columns from 'None' to 'Extreme'. The rows appear one by one, then the level columns. One tick lands per row for our patient (level 2 mobility, 1 self-care, 1 usual activities, 3 pain, 1 anxiety). The ticks are read off into the code 21131, written large under the grid with '3,125 states'. An arrow from the code into a box labelled 'Value set' (with 'public survey' under it), and out of it to a vertical q scale marked 1 'Full health', 0 'Dead' and a stretch below 0; the point q = 0.7 is marked on it. Then a mark at −0.594 below zero labelled 'UK 1997, 3L worst'. Quiz: The same patient's EQ-5D answers are scored in two countries and get different weights. Why? | Different value sets | Different questionnaires | The patient changed | correct: 1 | wrong hint: The ticks are identical — what else goes into the weight?
script: Last time, four years at q = 0.5 became 2 QALYs — but where does a weight like 0.5, or 0.7, actually come from?
It starts with a short questionnaire, and the most widely used one is the EQ-5D.
It asks about five dimensions of health: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression.
In the EQ-5D-5L version, each dimension has five levels, from no problems to extreme problems.
Our patient on the new treatment ticks one box per row — say, slight problems walking, moderate pain, and none on the rest.
The ticks become a five-digit code, here 2 1 1 3 1: one of 3,125 possible health states.
The code alone is not a weight: nobody has yet said how bad moderate pain is compared with trouble walking.
That is the job of a value set: a scoring formula estimated from a survey of the general public.
Members of the public value a sample of states, usually with the time trade-off, and a statistical model fills in the rest.
Feed in 21131, and the value set returns a weight — here, for illustration, 0.7.
The scale runs below zero too: in the 1997 UK value set for the older three-level version, the worst state scored minus 0.594.
So a weight joins two things: the patient describes the state, and the public says what it is worth.

parts.title: Time trade-off
parts.brief: The time trade-off turns a preference between years in a state and fewer healthy years into q.
parts.figure: Main figure: a QALY plot, quality of life q (0 to 1) against years (0 to 10), straight lines. Life A: a flat line at q = 0.7 for ten years, then death, labelled 'Life A: the state'. Life B: a flat line at q = 1, labelled 'Life B: full health', first drawn to ten years (a ghost), then shortened until it ends at seven years. At seven years, the area between them is shaded: green where B is above A (years 0–7, 'Quality gained') and red where A outlives B (years 7–10, 'Years given up'); the two areas are equal. Scratch card: q = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7 — temporary, gone after line 10. Quiz: Someone would give up 2 of 10 years to be free of a state. What is its weight? | 0.2 | 0.8 | 2.0 | correct: 2 | wrong hint: The weight is the share of years kept, not given up.
script: Now that we know the public values the states, how do you ask a person what a state is worth?
The time trade-off offers a choice between two lives.
Life A: ten years in the health state, then death.
Life B: years in full health, then death — and at first, the same ten years.
With equal years, everyone picks full health.
So shorten Life B, a year at a time, until the person can no longer choose between them.
Say that happens at seven years.
Then ten years in the state are worth seven healthy years.
The weight is the ratio: q = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.
On the figure, the two lives now enclose equal areas: the quality gained in the first seven years balances the three years given up.
That is the QALY idea run backwards: indifference means equal QALYs.
For a state some find worse than dead, the question is reframed — a spell in the state followed by full health, against dying now — and the weight comes out below zero.
So a time trade-off weight is the share of your years you would keep in full health, instead of living them all in the state.

parts.title: Standard gamble
parts.brief: The standard gamble turns a choice between a certain state and a risky cure into q.
parts.figure: Main figure: a decision tree. A decision square with two options. 'Certain' ends in a triangle 'The state', payoff 0.7 left unlabelled at first (shown as q). 'Gamble' leads to a chance circle with two branches: 'Full health' with probability p, payoff 1, and 'Dead' with probability 1 − p, payoff 0. The rollback value under the chance circle shows p × 1 + (1 − p) × 0. p is first shown at 1, then lowered to 0.7, where the gamble's value equals the certain state's 0.7. Explore: drag p and watch the gamble's value follow it; where it matches the certain state is the weight. Quiz: Someone accepts at most a 5% risk of death to be cured of a state. What is its weight? | 0.05 | 0.95 | 0.5 | correct: 2 | wrong hint: p is the chance of full health, not of death.
script: The time trade-off pays in years; the standard gamble pays in risk.
The choice: live on in the health state for certain,
or take a treatment that restores full health with probability p, and kills you with probability 1 − p.
If p is 1, the gamble is a free cure, and everyone takes it.
Lower p step by step, and at some point the person can no longer choose.
Say that point is p = 0.7.
The gamble is then worth 0.7 × 1 + 0.3 × 0, which is 0.7.
So the certain state is worth 0.7 too: the weight is read straight off the probability.
Pause and drag p: the gamble's value follows it, and where it matches the certain state is the weight.
Both methods put the state on the same scale, with full health at 1 and death at 0.
In practice, the same person usually gives a higher weight in the gamble than in the time trade-off — we come back to why.
So the standard gamble weighs a state by how much risk of death you would accept to escape it.

parts.title: Over time, to a cost per QALY
parts.brief: Weights times years, discounted, give incremental QALYs and the ICER for the running example; synthesis of the lecture.
parts.figure: Main figure: a grouped bar chart of QALYs per year, years 1 to 5 along the x axis, two series: 'Standard care' (0.5 in years 1–4, 0 in year 5) and 'New treatment' (0.7 in years 1–5). Readouts beside the legend: totals 2.0 and 3.5. Then a second stage: every bar shrinks to its discounted value at r = 3.5% (year one whole, year five at 87%: standard 0.50, 0.48, 0.47, 0.45; new 0.70, 0.68, 0.65, 0.63, 0.61), the undiscounted bars left as ghosts; the totals change to 1.90 and 3.27. Scratch card, one line as each is said: ΔQ = 3.27 − 1.90 = 1.37; ΔC = 30,000; ICER = 30,000 ÷ 1.37 ≈ 21,900 per QALY; vs λ = 30,000 — temporary, gone after line 12. Quiz: If the new treatment's extra benefit came 20 years from now instead of within five, what would discounting do to its ICER? | Raise it more | Lower it | Leave it unchanged | correct: 1 | wrong hint: A later year is divided by a bigger (1 + r) to the power t.
script: Now that each year has a weight, we can add up our running example over time.
Standard care: four years at 0.5, one bar per year, for 2.0 QALYs.
The new treatment: five years at 0.7, for 3.5 QALYs.
But a healthy year far in the future usually counts for less than one today, so future QALYs are discounted.
Each year is divided by (1 + r) to the power of how far away it is; NICE in England uses r = 3.5% for both costs and QALYs.
Watch the bars shrink: year one stays whole, and year five keeps 87% of its weight.
Summed, standard care falls to 1.90 QALYs, and the new treatment to 3.27.
The gain ΔQ shrinks from 1.5 to 1.37 QALYs.
The extra cost, ΔC = 30,000, is paid up front here, so it is not discounted.
The ICER is ΔC ÷ ΔQ: 30,000 ÷ 1.37, about 21,900 per QALY, up from 20,000.
A payer with a threshold λ of 30,000 per QALY would still say yes.
So a cost per QALY is a chain: ticks on a form, the public's trade-offs, weights times years, and a discount rate.
Every link is a choice someone made, and changing any one of them moves the ICER.
